0.title: Let the Peoples Praise You, O God
0.essay:
God’s plan has always been global. From the first promise to Abraham to the final vision of heaven, the Bible tells the story of God gathering worshippers from every people on earth.

From Abraham to Revelation

God promised Abraham, “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). And John saw the end of the story: “a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation” (Revelation 7:9). Everything in between is the unfolding of that plan.

Not an optional extra

Missions is not a hobby for a few enthusiastic Christians. It lies at the heart of God’s purpose and the church’s calling. Jesus’ last command was to “make disciples of all nations” (Matthew 28:19). Every Christian has a part to play: some go, many send, all pray.

A wider view

The Evangelism study focuses on sharing the faith with those around us. This study widens the view to the whole world. It traces God’s heart for the nations through Scripture, looks at the Great Commission and the mission in Acts, considers how Christians can go, send and pray, and ends with the goal: worship from every tribe and tongue.

The chapters

God’s Heart for the Nations; The Great Commission; The Mission in Acts; Going, Sending and Praying; and Every Tribe and Tongue.

For reflection

Does your concern for others stop at your own community, or does it reach to the nations?

1.title: God's Heart for the Nations
1.essay:
The Bible is not the story of a tribal god who cares only for one people. It is the story of the Creator of all peoples, who chose one nation in order to bless them all.

From the beginning

God created all humanity in his image and told them to fill the earth (Genesis 1:28). After the scattering at Babel, he did not abandon the nations. He called Abram and promised to bless him and make him a great nation. But the promise did not end with Abram: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Genesis 12:3). God’s plan of salvation was global from its first announcement.

Israel was chosen not instead of the nations, but for their sake. God told them, “you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6), representing God to the world. Too often Israel failed. But God’s purpose remained, and it was fulfilled in Christ, the true Israel.

The Psalms sing it

Israel’s worship looked ahead to the day when all nations would worship the LORD. “Declare his glory among the nations, his marvelous works among all the peoples!” (Psalm 96:3). Psalm 67 prays for God’s blessing on Israel, “that your way may be known on earth, your saving power among all nations” (Psalm 67:2). Then it calls the whole world to join in: “Let the peoples praise you, O God; let all the peoples praise you!” (Psalm 67:3). Israel’s blessing was meant to overflow.

A light for the nations

Through Isaiah, God spoke to his Servant: “It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6). The Messiah’s mission would reach far beyond Israel. Paul and Barnabas later quoted this verse to explain their mission to the Gentiles (Acts 13:47).

Foreigners in Israel’s story

The Old Testament repeatedly shows God’s grace reaching beyond Israel: Rahab of Jericho, Ruth the Moabite, the widow of Zarephath, and Naaman, commander of the Syrian army.

Naaman came to Israel seeking healing from leprosy because a captured Israelite servant girl had told his wife about the prophet Elisha (2 Kings 5:2–3). Through her simple witness, a foreign general came to confess, “Behold, I know that there is no God in all the earth but in Israel” (2 Kings 5:15).

Jonah

Jonah ran from God’s call to preach to Nineveh, Israel’s brutal enemy. Later he admitted why: “for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster” (Jonah 4:2). When Nineveh repented and God spared it, Jonah was angry.

God gave Jonah a plant for shade, then took it away, and Jonah was angry again. God’s final question reveals his heart: “And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?” (Jonah 4:11). The book ends with that question, unanswered, aimed at every believer. God cares for the nations, even when his people do not.

Mission begins with God

Mission is first God’s own work. The Father sent the Son, and the Father and the Son sent the Spirit. The church’s mission flows from that: “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21).

The glory of God

The ultimate goal of missions is the glory of God. Missions exists because worship does not yet fill the earth. But one day, “the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:14).

Think of a church that has always focused on its own neighbourhood. It begins studying God’s heart for the nations. Members start praying for unreached peoples and supporting a missionary family. Their vision of God grows, and so does their love for the world.

For reflection

What does Jonah teach you about God’s heart, and about your own? Which nation or people might God be putting on your heart?

2.title: The Great Commission
2.essay:
Before he ascended, the risen Jesus gave his disciples their marching orders. They still stand.

Imperfect followers

The eleven met the risen Jesus on a mountain in Galilee. “And when they saw him they worshiped him, but some doubted” (Matthew 28:17). The commission was given to imperfect followers, backed by a perfect Lord.

All authority

Jesus began: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). The commission rests on Christ’s universal authority. Because he is Lord of all, all nations must hear of him.

Make disciples

“Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28:19–20). The goal is not merely converts, but disciples: people who follow Christ, are baptised into his church and are taught to obey him.

The word “nations” refers to peoples — ethnic and language groups — not only countries. Christ’s commission reaches every people group on earth.

I am with you

“And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). The commission begins with Christ’s authority and ends with his presence. Missionaries and witnesses never go alone. And because he promised to be with his people to the end of the age, the commission was not only for the apostles. It continues until he returns.

Repentance and forgiveness

Luke records the commission differently. Jesus opened his disciples’ minds to understand the Scriptures: the Christ would suffer and rise, “and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47). The message is Christ crucified and risen, and the call is to repent and believe. And the disciples would not go in their own strength: they would be “clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49). Mission is rooted in Scripture and empowered by the Spirit.

Sent as Jesus was sent

In John, the risen Jesus appears to fearful disciples behind locked doors. He gives them peace, shows them his wounds, and says, “As the Father has sent me, even so I am sending you” (John 20:21). Then he breathes on them and says, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). The church continues Jesus’ mission in the world, flowing from his peace and the Spirit’s power.

I have many in this city

Reformed Christians believe God has chosen his people. Far from discouraging missions, this gives great confidence. When Paul faced opposition in Corinth, the Lord said to him in a vision, “Do not be afraid, but go on speaking and do not be silent, for I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many in this city who are my people” (Acts 18:9–10). Paul stayed a year and a half. God has people in every nation whom he will call, and our preaching is the means by which he gathers them.

The church’s central task

Making disciples of all nations is not one activity among many for the church. It is central to its reason for existing between Christ’s ascension and his return.

The disciples who received the commission were ordinary men, mostly fishermen, who had fled when Jesus was arrested. Within a generation, the gospel had spread across the Roman world. Christ’s authority and presence made the difference.

Think of a young couple, both professionals, who sense God calling them to serve among an unreached people. Their church tests the call, trains them and commits to send and support them. They go, trusting Christ’s promise to be with them.

For reflection

What is the difference between making converts and making disciples? How are you personally involved in the Great Commission?

3.title: The Mission in Acts
3.essay:
The book of Acts shows the Great Commission being carried out: the gospel spreading in widening circles, crossing every barrier, from Jerusalem to Rome.

Widening circles

When the disciples asked about the timing of the kingdom, Jesus redirected them to their task: “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth” (Acts 1:8). The rest of Acts unfolds that verse: Jerusalem (chapters 1–7), Judea and Samaria (chapters 8–12), and the wider world (chapters 13–28), ending with Paul preaching in Rome.

Breaking barriers

The gospel crossed every barrier. Samaritans, despised by Jews, received the word (Acts 8). An Ethiopian official was baptised on a desert road (Acts 8). Peter was sent to the house of Cornelius, a Roman centurion, and said, “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality” (Acts 10:34). The Spirit fell on Gentiles as he had on Jews. The church had to learn, sometimes painfully, that God’s people include every people.

Through persecution

After Stephen was killed, persecution scattered the believers. “Now those who were scattered went about preaching the word” (Acts 8:4). God used opposition to spread the gospel.

A sending church

The church at Antioch had a remarkably diverse leadership. “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them’” (Acts 13:2). “Then after fasting and praying they laid their hands on them and sent them off” (Acts 13:3). The first missionary journey began with a local church sending its best leaders. The missionaries were sent by the Holy Spirit and by the church together.

Missions in Acts is rooted in local churches. When Paul and Barnabas returned, they “gathered the church together” and “declared all that God had done with them, and how he had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles” (Acts 14:27).

Think of a small church that realises it has never sent anyone into missions. They begin praying, as Antioch did. Two years later a young member senses a call to Bible translation. The church commissions her, laying hands on her, and supports her for years.

Planting churches

Paul’s strategy was to preach in cities, plant churches, appoint elders and move on, later returning or writing to strengthen them. “And when they had appointed elders for them in every church, with prayer and fasting they committed them to the Lord in whom they had believed” (Acts 14:23). Missions is not only evangelism but church planting.

Guided by God

Paul and his companions were forbidden by the Spirit to preach in Asia, and prevented from entering Bithynia. Then Paul saw a vision of a man of Macedonia urging him, “Come over to Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16:9). They concluded that God had called them. God guides his mission through closed doors as well as open ones.

In Philippi, the first converts in Europe were a businesswoman named Lydia, a slave girl freed from an evil spirit, and a jailer and his household (Acts 16). The gospel reached the wealthy, the enslaved and the ordinary. The church in Philippi became Paul’s faithful partner in mission.

The Spirit drives mission

In Acts, the Holy Spirit empowers, directs and confirms the mission at every step. It depends on him, not on human strategy alone.

How will they hear?

Paul gives the logic of missions in Romans: “For ‘everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.’ How then will they call on him in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in him of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone preaching? And how are they to preach unless they are sent?” (Romans 10:13–15). “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans 10:17). Missions is necessary because people must hear.

Unfinished

Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance” (Acts 28:31). The story is left open. The mission continues through the church today.

For reflection

What barriers did the gospel cross in Acts, and what barriers must it cross today? What could your church learn from the church in Antioch?

4.title: Going, Sending and Praying
4.essay:
Every Christian has a part in missions. Some go, many send, and all pray.

Going

God calls some believers to leave home and take the gospel to other peoples. Paul wrote, “I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named, lest I build on someone else’s foundation” (Romans 15:20). He planned to go on to Spain, hoping the church in Rome would help him on his way. He combined pioneering zeal with dependence on supporting churches.

Missionaries today may be church planters, Bible translators, teachers, medical workers, or professionals who live and work among unreached peoples. Going is costly. But Jesus promised, “there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or lands, for my sake and for the gospel, who will not receive a hundredfold now in this time” (Mark 10:29–30).

Knowing the call

How does someone know whether God is calling them to go? Usually through a growing desire, godly character, relevant gifts, the confirmation of their local church, and open doors. The church should test and affirm such callings, as Antioch did (Acts 13:2–3).

Sending

Those who go need those who send. John praised Gaius for supporting travelling missionaries, even strangers: “You will do well to send them on their journey in a manner worthy of God” (3 John 6). And he drew the conclusion: “Therefore we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 8). Senders share in the work.

Senders give money, practical help, encouragement and friendship. The Philippian church supported Paul again and again, even when they were poor, and he thanked God “because of your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now” (Philippians 1:5). He called their gift “a fragrant offering, a sacrifice acceptable and pleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18), and assured them, “And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:19). Supporting missions is an act of worship.

Praying

When Jesus saw the crowds, “he had compassion for them, because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd” (Matthew 9:36). Then he said, “The harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few; therefore pray earnestly to the Lord of the harvest to send out laborers into his harvest” (Matthew 9:37–38). Compassion leads to prayer, and prayer leads to sending.

Paul asked churches to pray “that God may open to us a door for the word” (Colossians 4:3), and for boldness. Prayer is not the least we can do. It is essential.

Think of an elderly widow who cannot go abroad. She prays every day for the missionaries her church supports, writes them letters and gives sacrificially from her pension. When one of them returns home, he visits her first, and tells her that her prayers carried him through his hardest years.

Welcoming

Many people from other nations now live near us: students, migrants, refugees. Christians can reach the nations without leaving home, through hospitality and friendship. A meal, a lift, help with a form or a language can open a door to the gospel.

Unreached peoples

Many people groups still have little or no access to the gospel: no church, no Bible in their language, no Christian neighbour. Missions should give special priority to those who have never heard, as Paul did.

Faithfulness and fruit

Some missionaries see much fruit; others labour for years with little visible result. “Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). Faithfulness, not success, is what God requires. The harvest belongs to him.

For reflection

Are you a goer, a sender, or one who prays? Could you be more than one? Pray Matthew 9:38 for a specific missionary or people group this week.

5.title: Every Tribe and Tongue
5.essay:
The story of missions has a guaranteed ending. John was shown it, and it is glorious.

The goal

“After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation, from all tribes and peoples and languages, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palm branches in their hands” (Revelation 7:9). They cried out with a loud voice, “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10). Angels and elders fell on their faces in worship.

That is the goal of all missions: a worldwide people praising God for ever. And it will be achieved. Every people will be represented before the throne.

Ransomed by the Lamb

The new song of heaven celebrates the Lamb: “for you were slain, and by your blood you ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation, and you have made them a kingdom and priests to our God” (Revelation 5:9–10). Christ’s death is the price of a worldwide people. The cross is the foundation of missions, and its fruit is a church from every nation.

Before the end

Jesus warned that lawlessness would increase and love grow cold. But he also said, “And this gospel of the kingdom will be proclaimed throughout the whole world as a testimony to all nations, and then the end will come” (Matthew 24:14). History is moving towards the completion of the mission.

Only one way

Missions is urgent because salvation is found only in Christ. Peter, filled with the Spirit, told the very council that had crucified Jesus, “And there is salvation in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). Jesus himself said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

Some suggest that all religions lead to God, or that people can be saved without hearing of Christ. Scripture says otherwise. Sincere followers of other religions are not saved by their sincerity. They need to hear of Christ. That is not narrowness; it is the reason for urgency. The Apologetics study addresses this further.

Confidence

Because God has promised a people from every nation, missions cannot fail. Missionaries may suffer and die, as many have. But the gospel will reach the ends of the earth, and the Lamb will receive his reward.

Diversity in unity

The multitude in Revelation is not uniform. It is from every nation, tribe and language. God delights in the diversity of human cultures, redeemed and united in Christ. Heaven will not erase our differences, but gather them into one song.

At Pentecost, “devout men from every nation under heaven” (Acts 2:5) heard the gospel in their own languages. It was a foretaste of Revelation 7, the beginning of the reversal of Babel.

Think of a Bible translator who works for decades to translate the New Testament into the language of a small people group. When the first copies arrive, the believers there weep and sing as they read God’s word in their heart language for the first time. Another tribe has joined the song.

Joy

The goal of missions is the joy of the nations in God. “Let the nations be glad and sing for joy” (Psalm 67:4). Missions brings people the greatest good there is: knowing and enjoying God for ever.

Worship is the end

Missions is a means; worship is the end. When all the redeemed stand before the throne, missions will be over. But worship will last for ever.

For reflection

Does the vision of Revelation 7:9 move you? How could it shape your prayers and your giving? Choose one unreached people to pray for this month.
